source.title: Reproducible Scaling Laws for Contrastive Language-Image Learning
source.authors: Mehdi Cherti; R. Beaumont; Ross Wightman; Mitchell Wortsman; Gabriel Ilharco; Cade Gordon; Christoph Schuhmann; Ludwig Schmidt; J. Jitsev

record.file_problem: none; full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling trends in contrastive image-text pretraining and downstream vision tasks, extending scaling-law findings to a multimodal setting rather than testing language-model held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The reported fitted power laws concern downstream task error or retrieval performance, not held-out contrastive pretraining loss. Results cited from other studies and predictions without measured outcomes are not recorded as measured rows. Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and controlled comparisons of architectures at fixed parameter count are not tested.
record.test_reason: The authors train OpenCLIP models (ViT-B/32 to g/14) on LAION-80M/400M/2B for 3B–34B samples seen. They fit power laws of downstream error against total pretraining compute and compare the fits with OpenAI CLIP models trained on WIT. This is a new setting (contrastive image-text) with its own results on whether power-law scaling holds, whether downstream performance scales predictably, and how exponents depend on training data. Contrastive pretraining loss itself is never reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find power-law relations between scale (model, data, samples seen, fitted against total compute) and downstream performance in zero-shot classification, retrieval, linear probing and fine-tuning. OpenCLIP/LAION and OpenAI/WIT models scale differently by task, which the authors hypothesise comes from the pretraining data; batch-size differences are ruled out. Bottlenecks appear when one dimension is held fixed. They also extrapolate, e.g. 81.9% ImageNet zero-shot for ViT-G/14 at 68B samples, but do not verify these predictions.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains contrastive image-text models and fits laws to downstream classification and retrieval metrics; it does not use the original language-model held-out pretraining-loss measurement. It uses OpenCLIP and LAION alongside released OpenAI CLIP models trained on WIT.
record.method_sensitivity: Fitted scaling coefficients differ across downstream task and pretraining dataset. The paper reports bottleneck effects when data scale or samples seen is insufficient.
record.problems: The authors state that scale-space sampling is sparse, full hyperparameter tuning was not feasible, and additional OpenAI CLIP scale points were unavailable because WIT-400M is private. The main fit results are primarily presented in figures; there are no stated uncertainty intervals for the fitted coefficients.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-dataset linear-probe and fine-tuning results, as well as supplementary scaling plots for those tasks, were not separately extracted. They report downstream task results but do not test held-out pretraining loss; the main fitted classification and retrieval results and the bottleneck comparisons are retained.

untested.parts: Held-out contrastive (InfoNCE) pretraining loss vs parameters, data or compute is never reported; only downstream metrics are.
Extrapolations (e.g. 79.1% for g/14 at 34B, 81.9% for G/14 at 68B) are predictions with no measured large-run outcome to check them against. The study also does not concern loss.
No compute-optimal allocation is fitted; the authors list it as future work because sampling is too sparse.
No fixed-parameter comparison of shape. Fig 12 shows ResNet and ViT CLIP models follow similar trends, but not at matched parameter count.
Image/video generative models, repeated-data regimes, and power laws in pretraining loss for this modality are not tested.
Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss is not tested.
Fitting method (Pareto-frontier binning), parameter counting and schedule are not varied. Dependence is shown only across pretraining dataset and task.

missing.what: Power-law fits for few-shot and full linear probes on ImageNet, CIFAR-100 and VTAB (e.g. VTAB exponents -0.04 vs -0.06), bearing on downstream scaling and data-dependence
Fine-tuning scaling fits: ImageNet (-0.09 OpenCLIP vs -0.13 CLIP), robustness, and average of eight joint fine-tuned tasks (-0.16 vs -0.23); per-task fits vary widely
Retrieval data bottleneck: ViT-L/14 on LAION-400M barely improves from 13B to 34B samples (COCO 68.40 to 68.62), but does improve on LAION-2B
CLIP ResNet models on WIT show the same pattern of data-dependent exponents as CLIP ViTs (ImageNet -0.13, COCO -0.05)
Controls: batch-size changes move ImageNet accuracy 0.2–0.5 points, and trial-to-trial variance is about 0.4 points; the authors judge both too small to explain the trends

record.verdict_notes: No contrastive loss is reported, so V1–V3 are untested. V5 support rests on downstream error, not loss. WIT fits use only three models, and the compute range is narrow (about 1e11–1e12 GMAC). r9 had wrong numbers, now corrected. The bottleneck rows (r9–r14) bear on V6 only.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss as a function of model parameters, training tokens, or compute.
It fits laws to downstream performance and makes extrapolation predictions, but does not test whether small-run fits predict held-out pretraining loss on much larger runs.
No loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is measured for fixed compute.
The paper does not compare depth, width, or other architecture changes at fixed parameter count to measure their effect on loss.
Tests contrastive image-text pretraining and downstream vision tasks, not image/video generative models, repeated-data training as a general regime, or the other listed modalities.
Measures downstream task performance across scale; it does not test predictability across a broad set of downstream task types beyond those studied or the relation to pretraining loss.

Shows task- and training-distribution-dependent fitted slopes and bottleneck effects, but does not systematically vary fitting procedures or parameter-counting conventions, nor test published language-model laws against one another.

rows.subject: OpenCLIP ViT-B/32
rows.operation_detail: Compares zero-shot ImageNet accuracy across data scales at fixed samples seen.
rows.locator: Supplementary Table 19; bottleneck discussion in Section 4.1
rows.note: Accuracy improves, but the authors describe this lower-samples-seen setting as bottlenecked; the text says B/32 and B/16 show no change or deterioration at smaller samples-seen scales.
rows.check: Wrong baseline and value. Table 19 at 3B samples gives ViT-B/32 57.12% (LAION-400M) vs 57.36% (LAION-2B). The recorded 56.46 is LAION-80M at 13B and 62.53 is the 13B value. A +0.24 point change matches the authors' 'no change'. Bears on data-scaling gains, not V5/V7.

source_check.correct: At 3B samples seen, ViT-B/32 ImageNet accuracy is 57.12% on LAION-400M and 57.36% on LAION-2B. The recorded 56.46% belongs to LAION-80M at 13B samples; 62.53% belongs to LAION-2B at 13B samples. The absent state agrees with the authors' description of negligible improvement at smaller samples-seen scales.

relationships.condition: Contrastive image-text pretraining (OpenCLIP/LAION and CLIP/WIT); zero-shot classification and retrieval error vs total compute, over roughly 1–1.5 orders of magnitude
relationships.reason: Power-law fits on the Pareto frontier with negative exponents (-0.05 to -0.24) across ImageNet, robustness, COCO and Flickr (r1–r8). This is downstream error, not pretraining loss.
relationships.display_finding: Pareto-frontier downstream errors followed power laws with exponents from −0.05 to −0.24 across ImageNet, robustness evaluations, COCO, and Flickr.

source_check.reason: All eight reported frontier exponents are negative; Section 4 describes consistent improvement when scaling dimensions together. Table 19 also confirms the improvements at 34B samples in r11 and r14.

relationships.condition: Data scale increased (LAION-400M to 2B) while samples seen stays small (3B/13B) for ViT-B models
relationships.reason: Zero-shot ImageNet accuracy does not improve or drops (57.12 to 57.36; 63.23 to 62.53; 62.68 to 61.82). Gains in one dimension are hidden by a samples-seen bottleneck (r9, r10, r12).
relationships.display_finding: ImageNet accuracy changed from 57.12 to 57.36, 63.23 to 62.53, and 62.68 to 61.82, showing negligible or reversed gains under limited training exposure.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Data scale increased (LAION-400M to 2B) while samples seen stays small (3B/13B) for ViT-B models
source_check.reason: For this specific condition group, the authors describe no improvement or deterioration, and Table 19 confirms absent or reversed effects in r9, r10 and r12. V6 contains no bottleneck exception, so this group meets the rule for challenges; the jointly scaled setting retains its separate supports verdict.

relationships.condition: Same ViT architectures and near-matched recipe; LAION vs WIT pretraining data
relationships.reason: Exponents differ by data source and task, and the advantage flips. WIT is steeper on ImageNet (-0.16 vs -0.11) and robustness (-0.24 vs -0.13); LAION is steeper on COCO (-0.08 vs -0.05) and Flickr (-0.19 vs -0.10) (r1–r8).
relationships.display_finding: WIT has steeper exponents than LAION on ImageNet at −0.16 versus −0.11 and robustness at −0.24 versus −0.13, while LAION is steeper on COCO at −0.08 versus −0.05 and Flickr at −0.19 versus −0.10.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Same ViT architectures and near-matched recipe; LAION vs WIT pretraining data
source_check.reason: The fitted exponents differ across data sources and tasks, with the steeper slope switching from WIT for classification to LAION for retrieval. Attribution specifically to data remains the authors' hypothesis; compute-optimal allocation is untested.
